c.tagline: Sulfur baths and cobbled old-town charm

taxi.fareNote: official taxis white; most use Bolt/Yandex apps or agree fare

emergency.note: 112 is the unified emergency number for police, fire and ambulance; English-speaking operators are usually available.

hood_landmark.Old Town (Dzveli Tbilisi): Narikala Fortress above the sulfur-bath domes of Abanotubani
hood_landmark.Vake: Vake Park with its grand Soviet-era staircase and fountains
hood_landmark.Vera: the Dry Bridge flea market at the district's edge
hood_landmark.Saburtalo: Lisi Lake's promenade and swimming spots on its western edge
hood_landmark.Sololaki: the Mother of Georgia (Kartlis Deda) statue on the Sololaki ridge

avoid.reason: Very safe; do not attempt to enter the occupied regions of Abkhazia or South Ossetia

hood_desc: The historic core with sulfur bathhouses, cobbled lanes, wooden balconies, churches and the Narikala fortress; suits first-time visitors wanting atmosphere and walkable sights.
A prestigious, leafy district west of the center with upscale cafes, boutiques and Vake Park; suits well-heeled visitors and longer stays wanting a refined neighborhood.
A central bohemian-genteel district between Old Town and Vake, full of cafes, wine bars and galleries; suits younger travelers and creatives wanting a lively but residential base.
A modern residential and business district with wide avenues, malls and newer apartments; suits budget and longer-stay visitors wanting good value and metro links.
An elegant, fading-grand 19th-century quarter beside Old Town with ornate courtyards and trendy bars; suits travelers wanting character and a central spot slightly off the tourist track.

water.note: Tap water meets WHO standards and is safe to drink; some prefer bottled due to older building pipes.

transit.pay: Get a MetroMoney card (small deposit, sold at metro station kiosks and machines) and tap in at metro turnstiles or on buses; a 1 GEL fare covers 90 minutes of unlimited transfers (~$0.35-0.40). Cash and mobile-app payment are accepted but without the transfer discount.
transit.hours: Metro and buses run daily about 6am-midnight; there is no night service.

transit.m: Airport train to Central Station (twice daily), ~25 min

food.name: Khinkali
food.desc: Twisted soup dumplings of spiced meat or mushroom. Hold the topknot, bite a hole, drink the broth, and never eat the stem.

places.name: Pasanauri
places.note: Mountain-style khinkali done properly, with juicy broth and a queue of Georgians.

places.name: Zakhar Zakharich
places.note: Local favourite for cheap, huge dumplings and beer; unpretentious and always busy.

places.name: Sakhachapure No.1
places.note: Reliable all-rounder for khinkali and khachapuri under one roof; good for a first meal.

food.name: Khachapuri
food.desc: Cheese bread in many forms, from the Imeretian round to the boat-shaped Adjaruli topped with a raw egg and butter to stir in.

places.name: Retro
places.note: Old-school bakery-restaurant that Georgians name first for Adjaruli khachapuri.

places.name: Machakhela
places.note: Dependable chain specialising in the Adjaran boat; open late and everywhere.

places.name: Sakhachapure No.1
places.note: Serves the full regional range, Imeretian through Megrelian, in one sitting.

food.name: Mtsvadi
food.desc: Georgian barbecue: chunks of pork or veal skewered over grapevine embers, served with raw onion and tart tkemali plum sauce.

places.name: Shavi Lomi
places.note: Courtyard restaurant doing modern Georgian cooking; grilled meats and a good wine list.

places.name: Salobie Bia
places.note: Beloved for country cooking in clay pots; small dining room, so go early.

places.name: Racha
places.note: Cheap, smoky basement institution unchanged for decades; cash and patience required.

food.name: Badrijani nigvzit
food.desc: Fried aubergine slices rolled around a garlicky walnut paste and topped with pomegranate seeds. The star of any Georgian table.

places.name: Salobie Bia
places.note: Village recipes done with real care; the walnut dishes are the highlight.

places.name: Barbarestan
places.note: Cooks from a 19th-century Georgian cookbook; the most special-occasion meal in town.

places.name: Shavi Lomi
places.note: Refined plating of the classic cold starters in a leafy courtyard.

food.name: Lobio
food.desc: Kidney beans stewed with herbs and spices, served bubbling in a clay pot with mchadi cornbread and pickled vegetables.

places.name: Salobie Bia
places.note: Named for the dish; the clay-pot lobio with mchadi is the thing to order.

places.name: Racha
places.note: Old workers' basement serving lobio and chacha for a few lari.

places.name: Dezerter Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Market cooks ladle lobio out beside the spice and cheese counters.

food.name: Churchkhela
food.desc: Walnuts threaded on string and dipped again and again in thickened grape must until they set into a chewy candle-shaped sweet.

places.name: Dezerter Bazaar
places.note: Rows of churchkhela hanging over the stalls; the cheapest and freshest in the city.

places.name: Old Town stalls, Shardeni and Erekle II
places.note: Convenient if pricier, alongside dried fruit and spice blends for gifts.

places.name: Vino Underground
places.note: Serves churchkhela and cheese as a snack plate with natural wine flights.

food.name: Qvevri wine
food.desc: Wine fermented in buried clay qvevri as Georgians have done for 8,000 years, including the tannic orange whites made on their skins.

places.name: Vino Underground
places.note: Cellar bar founded by natural winemakers; the best place to understand qvevri wine.

places.name: 8000 Vintages
places.note: Wine shop and bar with hundreds of Georgian labels and staff who guide tastings.

places.name: g.Vino
places.note: Small natural-wine bar with a terrace, good cheese plates and rotating pours.

food.name: Chacha
food.desc: Fierce grape pomace brandy, the Georgian answer to grappa. Homemade versions appear at every supra toast.

places.name: Dezerter Bazaar
places.note: Homemade chacha sold from plastic bottles by the stallholders; taste before you buy.

places.name: Vino Underground
places.note: Stocks craft chacha from small producers, a big step up from the market stuff.

places.name: Racha
places.note: Cheap shots poured alongside lobio and mtsvadi in a classic basement tavern.

landmarks: Narikala Fortress
An ancient hilltop fortress spanning the 4th–17th centuries that offers the best panoramic views over Tbilisi's Old Town and the Kura River.
Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba Cathedral)
Georgia's largest and most iconic Orthodox cathedral, its golden dome and hilltop setting make it a dramatic photo subject especially at sunset.
Abanotubani Sulfur Bathhouses
The historic domed sulfur bath district beneath Narikala, known for its distinctive brick cupolas and colorful facades.
Anchiskhati Basilica
Tbilisi's oldest surviving church, a 6th-century stone basilica that captures the city's deep religious history.
Freedom Square
The bustling central square of Tbilisi, anchored by St. George's golden column, a classic shot of the modern city center.
Metekhi Church and Vakhtang Gorgasali Monument
A cliffside 13th-century church paired with an equestrian statue of Tbilisi's founder, a postcard view over the Old Town.
Mtatsminda Park
A hilltop amusement park reached by funicular that gives sweeping aerial views of the entire city.
Rustaveli Avenue
Tbilisi's grand historic boulevard lined with 19th-century architecture, theaters, and museums.
Bridge of Peace
A striking glass-and-steel pedestrian bridge over the Kura River that glows with LED lights at night, framed against Narikala Fortress.
Georgian National Museum
Home to priceless ancient gold artifacts and Soviet-era history, a key cultural landmark in the heart of the city.

train.note: Both international services are overnight sleepers from Tbilisi Central (Tbilisi Sadguri), on the north side of the city at the Station Square metro stop. The Yerevan train runs every second day, becoming nightly in the summer season from about mid-June to late September and less often in winter. The Baku overnight train has relaunched but is currently usable only by travellers who can enter Azerbaijan visa-free, which excludes many Western nationals, so check your eligibility before buying. Domestic trains, including the fast Stadler service to Batumi and the branch to Zugdidi for Svaneti, are booked on Georgian Railway's own ticketing site and sell out at weekends.

bus.note: Metro Turizm runs long-distance coaches between Tbilisi and Istanbul, roughly a day-long trip along the Black Sea coast and through the Sarpi border crossing. To Yerevan and Baku, transport is mostly frequent shared minibuses (marshrutkas) from the Ortachala and Avlabari stations rather than a bookable coach line, so you buy on the spot and leave when the vehicle fills. Carry your passport for all border crossings, and note that the Russian border at Larsi is subject to long queues and closures. Journey times are about 6 hours to Yerevan and 8-9 to Baku.

ferry.note: Tbilisi is inland with no ferries; international Black Sea passenger and vehicle ferries toward Bulgaria, Romania and occasionally Ukraine sail from Batumi and Poti on Georgia's coast, several hours west, and run to irregular cargo-led schedules, so contact the operator directly before relying on one.

half.name: Mtskheta
half.blurb: Ancient former capital with historic cathedrals sitting where two rivers meet below hilltop monastery.

half.name: Kakheti Wine Region
half.blurb: Rolling vineyards and old cellars in the cradle of Georgia's ancient winemaking tradition.

half.name: David Gareja
half.blurb: Cave monastery complex carved into desert hillsides along the remote Azerbaijan border.

half.name: Gori
half.blurb: Historic town beneath a hilltop fortress, birthplace of Stalin with its dedicated museum.

half.name: Uplistsikhe
half.blurb: Ancient rock-hewn cave city with tunnels and halls carved into a rocky ridge.

full.name: Kazbegi (Stepantsminda)
full.blurb: Mountain town where a lone church stands beneath the snowy peak of Mount Kazbek.
